Insights · Integration & Architecture

Modernizing legacy systems without replacing everything at once

Large replacement programs carry large risks. A step-by-step approach that uses integration to modernize around existing systems.

29 September 2026 · Hamerkop Systems · 2 min read

Institutions often depend on systems that are old, hard to change and still essential. Replacing them in a single program is tempting, but it concentrates risk: long timelines, complex data migration and a high-stakes cut-over. An alternative is to modernize progressively, using integration to connect new capabilities to existing systems and retiring old components when it is safe to do so.

1. Build an inventory of systems and interfaces

Document each system, what it is responsible for, who owns it and how it exchanges information today. Pay particular attention to informal interfaces: file transfers, scheduled scripts and manual re-keying between teams. These are often the most fragile links.

2. Put a controlled layer between systems

Instead of connecting every application directly to every other, introduce defined interfaces, such as APIs or a managed integration layer, through which systems exchange information. This separates consumers from the internal details of legacy platforms, so those platforms can later be changed or replaced without rewriting every connection.

3. Prioritize by value and risk

  • Which processes suffer most from the current limitations?
  • Which interfaces fail most often or need the most manual effort?
  • Where would a new capability, such as a digital channel or a reporting layer, deliver value quickly?

Start where the answer to these questions overlaps, and deliver improvements in small, testable steps.

4. Make integration observable

Integrations should not be invisible until they break. Monitoring of message flows, error rates and processing delays gives operations teams early warning and shortens investigations. Agreed service levels make expectations clear between teams and vendors.

5. Document for long-term ownership

Runbooks, interface specifications and support procedures turn an integration from a project deliverable into something the organization can operate. Without them, knowledge stays with individuals and every change becomes risky.

Institutional technology rarely lives in one system.

6. Retire deliberately

As functions move to new platforms behind the integration layer, legacy components can be switched off one at a time, with data archived according to retention requirements. Each retirement reduces cost and complexity without a single large cut-over.

The outcome

Progressive modernization lets institutions improve services while keeping operations running. The integration layer built along the way remains valuable: it becomes the foundation for connecting future systems, partners and government services.
